Voice typing works on Windows. It was the one thing 0.23 promised to keep hidden there rather than pretend to work: the transcription half had always been cross-platform, but the half that delivers the text — put it on the clipboard, press the paste chord into whatever app you were typing in — existed only for macOS. A session would listen, transcribe, and then drop the words on the floor, so the feature was switched off rather than shipped broken.

The delivery layer is written now. Hold **Ctrl+Alt+Space**, speak, release, and the text lands at your cursor in any app. Alt+Space could not be the trigger on Windows the way Option+Space is on macOS — it is the native window system menu — so the default moved, and anyone already carrying the old default in their settings is moved with it. Push-to-talk on Windows is key combinations only; the held-modifier triggers (fn, right ⌥, right ⌘, right ⌃) ride a macOS event tap with no counterpart, and the picker no longer offers them there.

Two limits, said out loud rather than hidden. Windows refuses injected keystrokes to a window running as administrator, so a paste into one of those reports itself as refused and the overlay tells you the text is waiting on your clipboard. And the loop that watches you correct a word and offers to remember it stays on macOS, because reading back the field we just pasted into needs an accessibility API Windows spells differently. The phrase dictionary still biases recognition on both platforms and is still editable by hand.

The Windows app has stopped showing you controls that do nothing. Settings hid its Permissions panel on Windows, which meant a Windows user whose microphone was set to Deny had no way to find that out from inside the app — the panel is there now, with the microphone row that Windows actually has. Onboarding no longer asks Windows users to grant macOS permissions. The voice-typing history no longer tells them to hold Option+Space. The find bar says Ctrl+F. The dictionary panel no longer sells a feature that platform does not have.

And the download page has stopped denying Windows exists. Parley has attached a Windows installer to every release since 0.23, and the site offered one button, labelled macOS, that handed everyone a `.dmg`. There are two buttons now, each honest about what it gives you: the Windows one says up front that this build records your microphone only, and that the installer is not code-signed yet, so SmartScreen will ask you to click through an unknown-publisher warning before it runs.

Capturing the other side of a call is still macOS-only. That is a Core Audio process tap, and the Windows equivalent — WASAPI loopback — remains unwritten. This release does not change that; it changes everything around it, so that what Windows *can* do is reachable, and what it cannot is stated where you will read it rather than buried in a release note from five versions ago.

macOS behaviour is unchanged.
